Modified assessment using the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) as context:
- Credit supply and demand: SLOOS indicates mixed credit dynamics—domestic banks reported softer demand for C&I loans, while foreign banks reported strengthened C&I demand. This points to lingering weakness for business credit domestically, partly offset by improvement among foreign bank clients.
- Lending standards: Large banks eased standards for several residential mortgage categories (GSE-eligible, QM jumbo, and QM non-jumbo/non-GSE), and small banks cited improved credit quality and competition as reasons for some easing. This suggests improving credit availability to households, consistent with accommodative financial conditions.
- Risk factors: Banks still cite the economic outlook, industry-specific problems, and lower risk tolerance as key reasons for tighter standards in some segments, indicating persistent caution around pandemic-sensitive sectors and small-firm credit.
- Policy interaction: The FOMC’s highly accommodative stance (ZLB, ongoing Treasury/MBS purchases) supports credit conditions, and SLOOS corroborates gradual easing on the household side. However, ongoing softness in domestic C&I demand and residual tightening pressures limit a broader positive shift.

Net tone: Slightly negative but moving closer to neutral versus the earlier FSR-based read, given modest easing in household credit and expectations for stronger consumer loan demand at small banks, tempered by weaker domestic C&I demand and continued caution.
